c081.front: SYSDATE or CURRENT_DATE: how do they differ?
c081.back: SYSDATE takes the time from the database server's operating system. CURRENT_DATE takes the time in your session's time zone. Both return the DATE type.
c081.try_sql:
-- SYSDATE: the server clock; CURRENT_DATE: the session time zone (compare with SESSIONTIMEZONE)
SELECT SYSDATE, CURRENT_DATE, SESSIONTIMEZONE FROM dual;

c082.front: TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE vs WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE: how do they differ?
c082.back: WITH TIME ZONE stores the time zone (an offset or a region) together with the value. WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE does not store it: it converts the value to DBTIMEZONE and shows it in your session's time zone when read.
c082.try_sql:
-- starts_at (WITH TIME ZONE) remembers its time zone; logged_at (WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE) is shown in the session time zone
SELECT e.event_id, TO_CHAR(e.starts_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI TZR') AS starts_at,
       e.logged_at, SESSIONTIMEZONE AS sesja
FROM   events e
WHERE  e.event_id IN (1, 3);

c083.front: What can EXTRACT take from a DATE value?
c083.back: Only YEAR, MONTH and DAY. HOUR, MINUTE and SECOND need a TIMESTAMP, for example EXTRACT(HOUR FROM CAST(d AS TIMESTAMP)). Otherwise you get ORA-30076.

c084.front: What do interval literals look like?
c084.back: INTERVAL '1-6' YEAR TO MONTH = 1 year and 6 months. INTERVAL '2 10:30:00' DAY TO SECOND = 2 days, 10 hours and 30 minutes. INTERVAL '90' MINUTE = 90 minutes.
c084.try_sql:
-- Three interval literals: 1 year 6 months, 2 days 10:30, 90 minutes
SELECT INTERVAL '1-6' YEAR TO MONTH AS a, INTERVAL '2 10:30:00' DAY TO SECOND AS b, INTERVAL '90' MINUTE AS c FROM dual;

c085.front: 31 January + 1 month: ADD_MONTHS or + INTERVAL MONTH?
c085.back: ADD_MONTHS(DATE '2024-01-31', 1) gives the last day of February (2024-02-29). + INTERVAL '1' MONTH raises ORA-01839, because 31 February does not exist.

c086.front: How do you show a TIMESTAMP in another time zone?
c086.back: ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Warsaw': the same instant, a different clock. FROM_TZ(ts, 'UTC') only attaches a zone to a plain TIMESTAMP (the time does not change). TZ_OFFSET('Europe/Warsaw') returns the offset from UTC, for example +01:00.
c086.try_sql:
-- AT TIME ZONE changes the clock (the same instant), FROM_TZ only attaches a time zone
SELECT TO_CHAR(TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 12:00:00 UTC' AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Warsaw', 'HH24:MI TZR') AS at_tz,
       TO_CHAR(FROM_TZ(TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 12:00:00', 'UTC'), 'HH24:MI TZR') AS from_tz,
       TZ_OFFSET('Europe/Warsaw') AS offset_dzis
FROM   dual;

c710.front: What type do TIMESTAMP - TIMESTAMP, DATE - DATE and TIMESTAMP + 1 give?
c710.back: TIMESTAMP - TIMESTAMP → INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND. DATE - DATE → NUMBER (a number of days). TIMESTAMP + 1 → DATE, because adding a number turns the result into a DATE.
c710.try_sql:
-- Result types: INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND, NUMBER (days) and DATE (no fractional seconds)
SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-03-10 12:00:00' - TIMESTAMP '2024-03-08 09:30:00' AS ts_minus_ts,
       DATE '2024-03-10' - DATE '2024-03-08' AS date_minus_date,
       TIMESTAMP '2024-03-10 12:00:00.5' + 1 AS ts_plus_1
FROM   dual;

c711.front: Which units do NUMTOYMINTERVAL and NUMTODSINTERVAL accept?
c711.back: NUMTOYMINTERVAL: 'YEAR', 'MONTH'. NUMTODSINTERVAL: 'DAY', 'HOUR', 'MINUTE', 'SECOND'. A wrong unit raises ORA-01760.

c712.front: INTERVAL '1' DAY + INTERVAL '1' MONTH: what happens?
c712.back: Error ORA-30081. YEAR TO MONTH and DAY TO SECOND intervals cannot be combined, because a month has no fixed number of days.
c712.try_sql:
-- Predict: can a day be added to a month?
SELECT INTERVAL '1' DAY + INTERVAL '1' MONTH FROM dual;

c713.back: Error ORA-01873. By default the first field of an interval may have only 2 digits. Write INTERVAL '123' DAY(3).

c714.front: EXTRACT(HOUR FROM ...) from a TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE: which hour does it return?
c714.back: The hour in UTC, not the local one. For example 23:30 in New York at UTC-4 gives 3. You get the local hour with TO_CHAR(ts, 'HH24').
c714.try_sql:
-- 23:30 in New York: EXTRACT gives the UTC hour, TO_CHAR the local one
SELECT TO_CHAR(e.starts_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI TZR') AS starts_at,
       EXTRACT(HOUR FROM e.starts_at) AS extract_hour,
       TO_CHAR(e.starts_at, 'HH24') AS local_hour
FROM   events e
WHERE  e.event_id = 3;

c715.front: What types do CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCALTIMESTAMP, SYSDATE and SYSTIMESTAMP return?
c715.back: CURRENT_DATE: DATE. CURRENT_TIMESTAMP: TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE. LOCALTIMESTAMP: TIMESTAMP. SYSDATE: DATE. SYSTIMESTAMP: TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE.
c715.try_sql:
-- Which values have a time zone (WITH TIME ZONE), and which do not?
SELECT CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, LOCALTIMESTAMP, SYSDATE, SYSTIMESTAMP FROM dual;

c1725.front: A global app: every user should see the same instant in their own time zone. Which data type?
c1725.back: TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE: it shows the time in the session's time zone by itself. If you want to keep the original time zone, use TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE.
c1725.try_sql:
-- logged_at (WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE) is shown in your session's time zone; next to it, the same instant in UTC
SELECT e.event_id, e.logged_at, SESSIONTIMEZONE AS sesja,
       TO_CHAR(SYS_EXTRACT_UTC(e.logged_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS utc
FROM   events e
WHERE  e.event_id IN (1, 3);

c1726.front: How are two TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE values compared and subtracted?
c1726.back: As instants in UTC, not as clock times. Example: on the day of the clock change in Warsaw, 03:00 CEST - 01:00 CET = +00 01:00:00, because only 1 hour passed.
c1726.try_sql:
-- The clock-change day in Warsaw: 2 hours on the clock, really only 1 passed
SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-03-31 03:00:00 Europe/Warsaw' - TIMESTAMP '2024-03-31 01:00:00 Europe/Warsaw' AS diff,
       CASE WHEN TIMESTAMP '2024-03-31 03:00:00 Europe/Warsaw' = TIMESTAMP '2024-03-31 01:00:00 UTC' THEN 'ta sama chwila' END AS cmp
FROM   dual;

c1727.front: FROM_TZ(ts, 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Warsaw': what does it do?
c1727.back: FROM_TZ says "this time is in UTC" and does not change the clock. Then AT TIME ZONE converts that instant to Warsaw. For example 12:00 UTC in July → 14:00 (summer time, UTC+2).
c1727.try_sql:
-- 12:00 UTC in July is 14:00 in Warsaw (summer time)
SELECT TO_CHAR(FROM_TZ(TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 12:00:00', 'UTC'), 'HH24:MI TZR') AS utc,
       TO_CHAR(FROM_TZ(TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 12:00:00', 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Warsaw', 'HH24:MI TZR TZD') AS warsaw
FROM   dual;

c1728.back: The text '+05:30'. India has no daylight saving time. For regions with daylight saving time, the result depends on today's date.
c1728.try_sql:
-- Kolkata is always +05:30; the result for Warsaw depends on today's date
SELECT TZ_OFFSET('Asia/Kolkata') AS kolkata, TZ_OFFSET('Europe/Warsaw') AS warsaw FROM dual;

c1729.front: EXTRACT(SECOND FROM ...) from a TIMESTAMP: what does it return?
c1729.back: The seconds including the fraction, for example 30.5. From a DATE only YEAR, MONTH and DAY may be extracted (otherwise ORA-30076).

c1730.front: From which values does EXTRACT take TIMEZONE_HOUR?
c1730.back: From a TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, for example SYSTIMESTAMP or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. LOCALTIMESTAMP and a plain TIMESTAMP have no time zone: you get ORA-30076.

c1731.front: Which text formats does TO_DSINTERVAL accept?

c1732.back: +02-06. The fraction turns into months: 2.5 years = 30 months = 2 years and 6 months.
c1732.try_sql:
-- Predict: 2.5 years as YEAR TO MONTH
SELECT NUMTOYMINTERVAL(2.5, 'YEAR') AS i FROM dual;

c1733.front: What does EXTRACT(MONTH FROM INTERVAL '30' MONTH) return?
c1733.back: 6. The literal becomes +02-06 (2 years and 6 months), and EXTRACT returns one field, not the total of all months.
c1733.try_sql:
-- 30 months is +02-06: EXTRACT(MONTH) gives 6, not 30
SELECT INTERVAL '30' MONTH AS i,
       EXTRACT(YEAR FROM INTERVAL '30' MONTH) AS y,
       EXTRACT(MONTH FROM INTERVAL '30' MONTH) AS m
FROM   dual;

c1734.front: How do you get the last day of the previous month without ORA-01839?
c1734.back: ADD_MONTHS(d, -1) for month-end dates, or TRUNC(d, 'MM') - 1. Note: DATE '2024-03-31' - INTERVAL '1' MONTH raises an error, because 31 February does not exist.

c1735.front: An INTERVAL DAY(2) TO SECOND(0) column: what if the value is too large? And if it has too many fractional seconds?
c1735.back: A first field that is too large (for example 120 days) → error ORA-01873. Too many fractional seconds → the value is rounded to the SECOND(p) precision, without an error (15.75 s → 16 s).

c1736.front: duration > 1 on an INTERVAL column: does it work?
c1736.back: No, error ORA-00932: Oracle does not convert a NUMBER to an INTERVAL by itself. Write duration > INTERVAL '1' DAY.
